blocks.html: An input device sends data and instructions into the computer. It converts what we type, point, speak or show into binary signals.
The most common input device. Most keyboards follow the QWERTY layout, named after the first six letters of the top row. Its keys fall into groups:

rows: Special tasks: F1 opens Help, F5 refreshes, F2 renames
Used with other keys: Ctrl + C copies, Ctrl + V pastes
Arrow keys, Home, End, Page Up, Page Down
Fast number entry, as in a bank or shop
Enter, Esc, Backspace, Delete, Tab, Caps Lock, Space bar

blocks.html: Did you know? Indian languages can be typed with the InScript keyboard layout, which is built into Windows and Android. The Government of India recommends it for typing Hindi in offices.

items.html: Mouse — moves a pointer on the screen. Actions: click (select), double-click (open), right-click (shortcut menu), drag and drop (move), scroll (move up/down). Modern mice are optical (use a light beam) and often wireless.
Touchpad (trackpad) — the flat pad on a laptop that works like a mouse.
Touchscreen — both input and output: you touch the screen to select. Used in mobiles, ATMs, railway enquiry kiosks.
Joystick — a stick for games and flight simulators.
Light pen and stylus — for drawing directly on a screen or a graphics tablet.

rows: Converts a paper document or photo into a digital image
Scanning certificates for an online admission form
Billing counters in supermarkets and medical shops
UPI payments, train tickets, Aadhaar letters
Competitive exams such as JEE, NEET and board objective papers
Printed text from an image, turned into editable text
Numbers printed in magnetic ink at the bottom of cheques
Aadhaar authentication, ration shops (ePoS), office attendance

items.html: Microphone — records voice; used for voice typing and voice assistants.
Webcam — a small video camera for online classes and video calls.
Digital camera — captures photos and videos and stores them on a memory card.

blocks.html: An output device shows or gives the result of processing in a form humans can understand.

items.html: Soft copy — output shown on a screen or played as sound; it cannot be touched and disappears when the device is off.
Hard copy — output printed on paper; it can be carried and kept.

blocks.html: The picture on a monitor is made of tiny dots called pixels (picture elements). The number of pixels across and down is the resolution — for example 1920 × 1080 (Full HD). More pixels mean a sharper picture. Screen size is measured diagonally in inches.

rows: Old, heavy and bulky, used a lot of power
LCD lit by Light Emitting Diodes
Brighter, thinner and more power-efficient than LCD; most common today
Organic LED, each pixel makes its own light
Deep blacks, very thin, used in premium phones and TVs
A head strikes an inked ribbon against paper
No physical striking; use ink spray, laser or heat
Can print several carbon copies at once
Example: dot matrix — used for bank passbooks and multi-copy bills

items.html: Inkjet printer — sprays tiny drops of ink; good for colour photos at home.
Laser printer — uses a laser and toner powder; fast and sharp, used in offices and schools.
Thermal printer — uses heat on special paper; used for ATM slips, shop bills and parking tickets.
Plotter — draws large, precise drawings such as building maps and engineering designs.
3D printer — builds solid objects layer by layer from plastic or other materials.
Speakers and headphones — sound output.
Projector — shows the screen on a large wall; used in smart classes.

blocks.html: Primary (main) memory is directly accessed by the CPU.

items.html: Holds the programs and data that are being used right now.
It is volatile: everything in it is lost when the power goes off. That is why unsaved work is lost in a power cut.
More RAM lets you run more programs together without slowing down. Typical sizes today: 8 GB or 16 GB in laptops.
Types: DRAM (dynamic, cheaper, used as main memory) and SRAM (static, faster, used as cache).
Holds permanent instructions, such as the BIOS/UEFI that starts the computer (booting).
It is non-volatile: contents remain without power.
Types: PROM (programmed once), EPROM (erased with ultraviolet light), EEPROM (erased electrically; flash memory is a kind of EEPROM).

blocks.html: Cache memory — a very fast, small memory between the CPU and RAM. It keeps the data the CPU uses most often, so the CPU does not have to wait for RAM.
Secondary storage keeps data permanently, even without power, and holds much more than RAM.

rows: Spinning metal platters and a moving head; cheap per GB
No moving parts; much faster, quieter and tougher than HDD
Small, portable, plug into USB or phone
Read by a laser; mostly old software and music
Files on internet servers; Google Drive, OneDrive, DigiLocker

blocks.html: Did you know? DigiLocker, a Government of India service, lets you keep official copies of your Aadhaar, PAN, driving licence and board mark sheets in the cloud. Many boards issue digital mark sheets there.

rows: Example: HDD, SSD, pen drive, DVD

blocks.html: A port is a socket on the computer where a device is plugged in.

rows: Keyboard, mouse, pen drive, printer, phone charging
Monitor, TV or projector with video and sound
Wireless mouse, earbuds, internet without cables

blocks.html: Aim: To use input/output devices and measure storage.

items.html: Keyboard practice. Open Notepad. Type your name and address. Try: Caps Lock, Shift + a letter, Backspace, Delete, Home, End and Ctrl + A (select all).
Mouse actions. On the desktop, practise single-click, double-click (open This PC), right-click (see the shortcut menu), and drag an icon to a new place.
Check storage. Open File Explorer → This PC. For drive C:, write the total size and free space. Insert a pen drive and note its size too.
Copy to a pen drive. Save your Notepad file, then copy it to the pen drive. Use Safely Remove Hardware before pulling it out.
Storage arithmetic. If one phone photo is about 4 MB, how many photos fit in a 32 GB pen drive? (32 × 1024 ÷ 4 = 8192 photos.)
Print preview. Open your file and press Ctrl + P to see the print preview. Note the printer name and whether it is inkjet or laser.

blocks.html: Record: Draw the memory hierarchy (Figure 2.1) and write one device from your lab at each level.

items.html: Input devices send data into the computer: keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, scanner, barcode/QR reader, OMR, OCR, MICR, biometric scanner, microphone and webcam.
Output devices give results: monitors (soft copy), printers (hard copy), speakers, projectors, plotters and 3D printers.
Impact printers strike a ribbon (dot matrix); non-impact printers use ink, laser or heat.
RAM is fast and volatile; ROM is permanent and holds start-up instructions; cache sits between CPU and RAM.
Secondary storage is permanent: HDD (magnetic), SSD and pen drives (solid state), CD/DVD/Blu-ray (optical) and cloud storage.
Ports such as USB, HDMI and Ethernet connect devices to the computer.
